TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables  
for Dynamic Speculative Decoding

 

Abhishek Malvankar ¹  Paul Castro ¹  Nick Mitchell ¹  Lionel Villard ¹ 

^(†)^(†)footnotetext: ¹IBM Research. Correspondence to: Abhishek
Malvankar \<asmalvan@us.ibm.com\>, Paul Castro \<castrop@us.ibm.com\>,
Nick Mitchell \<nickm@us.ibm.com\>, Lionel Villard
\<villard@us.ibm.com\>.  
Preprint.

###### Abstract

Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only
while the GPU has spare compute, so the best _draft length_, the number
of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows.
vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a
hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We
present TableTune. Its _tuner_ times the decoding step for every batch
size and draft length on vLLM’s own serving path and computes, in
minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its _controller_, a vLLM
plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and
rebuilds the table while serving. We measure TableTune only against
other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least
94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in
four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator
having to know which length that is. Against reimplementations of
TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case
loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3%
against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM’s documented
table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. Starting from
mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to
45% on vLLM’s default runner), and after a workload switch with the
DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table’s loss. In llm-d’s
optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four
GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3
and up to 25% faster than vLLM’s documented table at high load, and the
controller raises the documented table’s throughput by up to 29%.

## 1 Introduction

Generating text with an LLM is slow because it is sequential: each new
token requires a full pass through the model, and each pass mostly waits
on reading the model’s weights from GPU memory [Pope et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib30). *Speculative decoding* [Leviathan et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib14); [Chen et al. (2023)](#bib.bib3) hides part of this
cost. A small, fast _drafter_ guesses the next few tokens; the _target
model_ checks all guesses in one pass, keeps those it agrees with, and
adds one token of its own. Because every kept token is verified, the
output is exactly what the target would have produced alone.

Speculation is not free. Every guess is extra work, and wrong guesses
are thrown away. On an idle GPU the extra work is nearly free, because
the GPU waits on memory anyway; on a busy GPU serving many requests it
slows every step, and speculation can make serving slower than not
speculating [Liu et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib24). The best number of guesses
per step, the _draft length_, therefore depends on load.

vLLM [Kwon et al. (2023)](#bib.bib13) recently added _Dynamic
Speculative Decoding_ (Dynamic SD) [Ranjan (2026)](#bib.bib33), which
lets the draft length depend on the _batch size_, the number of requests
in a step. The operator supplies a table such as “batch sizes 1–64:
guess 3 tokens; 65–128: guess 1; above: none.” The table is written by
hand, often copied from the documentation, and nothing checks or
corrects it. Users report throughput collapsing when the batch
oscillates around a table edge [tobby168 (2026)](#bib.bib38) and Dynamic
SD running 21–31% slower than no speculation on an H100 [seongyun1104
(2026)](#bib.bib36).

#### TableTune.

TableTune keeps vLLM’s mechanism and makes its table measured and
self-correcting (Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4 Design")). Its tuner
runs once per GPU, engine, model and drafter: it times one decoding step
for a grid of batch sizes and every draft length through vLLM’s own
serving path, measures how often guesses are accepted, and computes the
table that maximizes useful tokens per second at every batch size. Its
controller, a vLLM plugin that needs no engine changes, re-estimates
acceptance from live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving. Both
emit vLLM’s own table format. Prior work established the ingredients:
TurboSpec [Liu et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib24) chooses the draft length that
maximizes goodput from profiled step times, [Su et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib37) make it depend on the batch size, and Nightjar [Li
et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib16) learns it online. TurboSpec and Nightjar
change the engine’s decisions; TableTune instead makes vLLM’s existing
production table measured and self-correcting, with step times measured
on the serving path rather than fitted, a controller that runs as a
plugin, and a three-GPU study of what that table can deliver and what it
needs from the engine.

## 2 Background

#### Batches and decoding.

A serving engine runs one forward pass over a _batch_ of requests per
_step_; the _batch size_ $`B`$ is the number of requests in it. With
*continuous batching* [Yu et al. (2022)](#bib.bib44) requests join and
leave every step, so $`B`$ follows the traffic. Our benchmarks set the
_concurrency_ $`c`$, the number of open requests. The live batch, vLLM’s
count of running requests, is smaller: on average about half to two
thirds of $`c`$ in our closed-loop runs. Tables are indexed by the live
batch; our figures plot $`c`$. In a decode step the GPU reads every
weight once, so with few tokens per step the step time is set by memory
bandwidth and extra tokens cost little, up to the *ridge
point* [Williams et al. (2009)](#bib.bib40) (about 200 tokens per step
on a T4, 210 on an A10G and 300 on an H100 SXM).

#### Speculative decoding.

A drafter proposes $`k`$ tokens. The target scores them in one pass and
accepts guesses up to the first disagreement, then appends one token of
its own [Leviathan et al. (2023)](#bib.bib14); [Chen et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib3). With $`a_{i}`$ the probability that guess $`i`$ and
all before it are accepted, the expected _tokens per step_ is
$`\tau(k)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}`$. EAGLE-style drafters [Li et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib17); [Li et al. (2024c)](#bib.bib18); [Li et al.
(2025b)](#bib.bib19) are small heads on the target’s features; a _draft
model_ is a separate small LLM; _n-gram_ drafting [Saxena
(2023)](#bib.bib35) copies prompt text; DFlash [Chen et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib4) drafts a block of tokens in one pass of a small
diffusion model.

#### Goodput.

We maximize _goodput_, kept tokens per second [Liu et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib24): the tuner predicts it with
Equation [1](#S2.E1 "In Goodput. ‣ 2 Background"), and we measure it as
output tokens per second (throughput). With step time $`T(B,k)`$,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       G(B,k)=B\cdot\tau(k)\,/\,T(B,k).
       ```                               |     | (1) |

Speculation raises the numerator and the denominator; whether it pays
depends on which grows faster at that $`B`$.

#### vLLM Dynamic SD and CUDA graphs.

vLLM takes a table num*speculative_tokens_per_batch_size of ranges
$`[B*{\text{start}},B\_{\text{end}},k]`$ and looks up $`k`$ for each
step [Ranjan (2026)](#bib.bib33); the documentation’s example is
$`[[1,64,3],[65,128,1],[129,512,0]]`$. A *CUDA graph* [NVIDIA
(2025b)](#bib.bib29) replays a recorded sequence of kernels with one
launch, saving CPU launch time. With a table, vLLM’s default V1 model
runner replaces its _full_ decode graphs with _piecewise_ graphs,
because the tokens per request now vary; its V2 runner keeps full graphs
per draft length since October 2026 [yewentao256 (2026)](#bib.bib43).

## 3 Motivation

Figure 1: No fixed draft length is best at every load. H100 (V2 runner),
Qwen3-4B + EAGLE-3, code prompts at temperature 1.0, mean of three runs:
throughput as % of the best fixed draft length at each load.

Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Motivation") shows the problem on an
H100 with Qwen3-4B [Qwen Team (2025)](#bib.bib32) and its EAGLE-3
drafter [Li et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib19). _The best length changes with
load:_ length 3 is best at low load and length 1 at 128 requests; fixed
length 1 loses 15% at 1 request and length 3 loses 12% at 128. _The best
table changes with the GPU and the engine:_ the tuned tables are
$`[[1,18,3],[19,43,2],[44,128,1]]`$ on a T4,
$`[[1,16,3],[17,60,2],[61,91,1],[92,128,0]]`$ on an A10G and
$`[[1,50,3],[51,128,2]]`$ on the H100 with the V2 runner; the H100’s
plain step grows only from 4.4 to 6.1 ms between a batch of 1 and 128,
the T4’s from 35.7 to 92.3 ms. _The engine decides whether any table can
pay:_ on the default V1 runner a table costs about 40% of the throughput
at low load
(Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.2 Q1: measured tables against fixed lengths ‣ 6 Evaluation")).
_Acceptance changes with the traffic:_ EAGLE-3’s tokens per step at
length 3 range from 1.81 (translation) to 2.43 (math) across seven
Spec-Bench [Xia et al. (2024)](#bib.bib42) and code workloads, on every
GPU we measured.

These observations suggest a split. Step time depends on hardware,
engine and batch size, is stable, and can be measured once offline.
Acceptance depends on traffic, drifts, and should be tracked online.
TableTune follows this split.

## 4 Design

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: TableTune. The tuner measures step time on vLLM’s serving path
and acceptance on sample prompts, and writes a table in vLLM’s own
format. While serving, the controller plugin reads vLLM’s acceptance
counters, re-estimates acceptance and rebuilds the table with the
tuner’s step times.

### 4.1 The tuner

#### Step time.

Let $`K`$ be the longest draft length the server may use, vLLM’s
num*speculative_tokens (3 for EAGLE-3, 5 for n-gram and the draft model,
8 for DFlash). For each draft length $`k`$ from 0 to $`K`$ the tuner
starts vLLM with the real drafter and a one-range table
$`[[1,B*{\max},k]]`$, so the timed path is exactly the serving path,
including the graph mode the server will use. For each batch size $`B`$
it sends $`B`$ prompts of the workload’s typical length (32 tokens by
default) twice, asking once for 1 output token and once for 65; the
difference is 64 decode steps, so $`T(B,k)=(t*{65}-t*{1})/64`$. It keeps
the median of three repeats, over every batch size up to 16 and then in
steps of 4 to 8 up to $`B\_{\max}`$. To keep the batch fixed while
timing, it uses vLLM’s test mode that rejects every guess: each step
does the full drafting and verification work of length $`k`$, but all
$`B`$ requests advance one token per step and finish together. The
benefit of accepted guesses is added back through $`\tau(k)`$. Work that
grows with the number of accepted tokens is not timed this way;
Section [6.7](#S6.SS7 "6.7 Q6: cost and reliability of measuring ‣ 6 Evaluation")
measures what that misses.

#### Acceptance.

The tuner then measures how often guesses are accepted. It runs the
drafter at the longest length, $`K`$ guesses per step, on 160 sample
prompts, at the temperature the server will use, and reads vLLM’s own
published speculative-decoding metrics, vllm:spec*decode_num_drafts and
vllm:spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens_per_pos: how many drafts were made
and, for every position $`i`$, how many of them kept guess $`i`$. Their
ratio is $`a*{i}`$. One run covers every shorter length too, because a
draft of length $`k`$ is just the first $`k`$ guesses of a draft of
length $`K`$.

#### The table.

For each batch size $`B`$ the tuner computes the goodput of every draft
length (Equation [1](#S2.E1 "In Goodput. ‣ 2 Background")) and picks the
highest. Two rules keep the table short. It keeps the previous batch
size’s length unless another is more than 0.5% better, so near-ties do
not create edges, and it merges any range narrower than 25% of its first
batch size into a neighbour. Some drafters guess only on some steps:
n-gram drafts only when the text it has seen contains a match. For them
the tuner multiplies acceptance by the share of steps with a guess, the
_proposal rate_, but still charges the full step time $`T(B,k)`$, since
a step in which some requests draft costs about as much as one in which
all do. From the same profiles, a GPU-free _screening_ predicts each
fixed length’s worst loss, so an operator can keep a fixed length when a
table would not help.

### 4.2 The controller

The controller is a vLLM general plugin that answers the scheduler’s
draft-length lookup. It learns acceptance from live traffic and turns it
into a table.

#### What it observes.

The controller adds no instrumentation of its own. After every step it
receives the counts that vLLM’s scheduler records for those same
published metrics: for each request, how many guesses were drafted
($`d`$) and how many were accepted ($`m`$; verification stops at the
first wrong guess, so the accepted guesses are always the first $`m`$).
The controller keeps two counts per draft position $`i`$:
$`\text{drafted}_{i}`$, the number of drafts that reached position $`i`$
($`d\geq i`$), and $`\text{accepted}_{i}`$, the number in which guess
$`i`$ was accepted ($`m\geq i`$). A request that drafts 3 guesses and
keeps 2 adds one to $`\text{drafted}_{1..3}`$ and to
$`\text{accepted}_{1..2}`$. The ratio
$`\text{accepted}_{i}/\text{drafted}_{i}`$ estimates $`a_{i}`$, the
probability that the first $`i`$ guesses are all accepted.

#### From acceptance to draft length.

Acceptance sets what each extra guess is worth: since
$`\tau(k)=1+\sum_{i\leq k}a_{i}`$, going from length $`k-1`$ to $`k`$
gains $`a_{k}`$ tokens per step and costs $`T(B,k)-T(B,k-1)`$. The gain
falls with $`k`$ because $`a_{k}`$ falls, and the cost grows with $`B`$,
so for each $`B`$ the best length is where the next guess stops paying,
the maximum of Equation [1](#S2.E1 "In Goodput. ‣ 2 Background"). Higher
acceptance therefore keeps long drafts up to larger batches; lower
acceptance moves the table’s edges to smaller batches and shorter
lengths, down to length 0. The step times never change while serving, so
acceptance is the only input the controller updates.

#### Estimating and rebuilding.

Every $`N`$ steps it computes
$`\hat{a}_{i}=(w\,a_{i}^{\text{prior}}+\text{accepted}_{i})/(w+\text{drafted}_{i})`$,
a blend of the tuner’s values (worth $`w=2000`$ observations) and the
live counts, which fade by half after each rebuild so recent traffic
dominates, and rebuilds the table from
Equation [1](#S2.E1 "In Goodput. ‣ 2 Background") with the tuner’s step
times. A position that is never drafted keeps its prior: while the table
runs length 1 or 0 the controller learns nothing about later guesses.
Two options matter when the traffic changes: _exploration_ (one step at
the longest allowed length every 50 steps, so every position keeps being
observed) and _prior decay_ (the prior’s weight also halves at each
rebuild). Near a table edge it holds the current length while the batch
size is within $`h`$ of the edge (_hysteresis_), avoiding the
oscillation of [tobby168 (2026)](#bib.bib38). By default it uses only
the lengths in its starting table, which have profiles and captured
graph sizes; under V1 an opt-in mode allows any profiled length, while
under V2 only the starting table’s lengths have full CUDA graphs.

## 5 Implementation

TableTune is about 1,880 lines of Python with 104 test functions. The
tuner is one command (dsd-tuner run). Because the table is a vLLM
argument and the controller an installed plugin enabled by environment
variables, TableTune needs no engine changes and deploys into serving
stacks such as llm-d by configuration alone. The tuner runs unchanged on
vLLM’s V1 and V2 runners. Code, per-GPU tables, benchmark scripts, raw
results and analysis scripts are available at
[https://github.com/asm582/tabletune](https://github.com/asm582/tabletune).

## 6 Evaluation

We answer six questions. _Q1_
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Q1: measured tables against fixed lengths ‣ 6 Evaluation")):
does a measured table hold up against every fixed draft length, across
loads, drafters and GPUs? _Q2_
(Section [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Q2: against prior adaptive control ‣ 6 Evaluation")):
how does it compare with prior adaptive controllers? _Q3_
(Section [6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Q3: the controller ‣ 6 Evaluation")): does
the controller repair mistuned tables and follow a workload change? _Q4_
(Section [6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5 Q4: end to end in llm-d ‣ 6 Evaluation")):
do the gains carry over to a production stack like llm-d? _Q5_
(Section [6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Q5: what the engine must provide ‣ 6 Evaluation")):
what must the engine provide? _Q6_
(Section [6.7](#S6.SS7 "6.7 Q6: cost and reliability of measuring ‣ 6 Evaluation")):
what does TableTune cost, and how reliably can step times be measured?

### 6.1 Setup

#### Hardware and software.

Our main platform is an H100 80 GB SXM (3.35 TB/s, BF16) on an OpenShift
cluster, a whole GPU with a 16-CPU quota on a Xeon 8480+ host. We ran
the main matrix of tuner, sweep and controller experiments twice on it:
with vLLM 353e491ef and its default V1 runner, and with a vLLM nightly
(43b4aaea, October 2026) and the V2 runner, which keeps full CUDA graphs
per draft length. Because a table cannot pay under V1
(Section [6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Q5: what the engine must provide ‣ 6 Evaluation")),
all later studies use V2 only. The repository lists every study with its
scripts, tables and raw results. For comparison we ran the same
experiments, with the same scripts, prompts and loads and vLLM’s V1
runner, on a Tesla T4 (FP16) and an A10G (BF16), both AWS instances with
2-core hosts. Targets are Qwen3-4B, its 4-bit AWQ version [Lin et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib21), the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B [Qwen Team
(2025)](#bib.bib32) and, in llm-d, Qwen3-32B at TP=2 and Qwen3-8B;
drafters are EAGLE-3, n-gram, Qwen3-0.6B as a draft model, and DFlash.

#### Workloads and load.

AIPerf [NVIDIA (2025a)](#bib.bib28) keeps $`c`$ requests open in a
closed loop; a _sweep_ measures every load $`c`$ from 1 to 128, with
$`4c`$ requests per level after $`c`$ warm-up requests, and the maximum
batch is 128. The main workload is _code_: InstructCoder [Li et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib15) instructions (about 32 prompt tokens), answers up
to 256 tokens, temperature 1.0. n-gram uses _code-apply_ (an instruction
plus the code to edit, about 151 tokens in, answers up to 512 tokens,
greedy); the chat study uses Spec-Bench (greedy, up to 64 requests).

#### Isolation and statistics.

Each H100 V1 study ran alone on an otherwise idle node, because
piecewise CUDA graphs turned out to be sensitive to host contention
(Section [6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Q5: what the engine must provide ‣ 6 Evaluation"));
the V2 studies ran on nodes shared with other teams’ GPU jobs, which
full graphs are insensitive to ($`\pm`$4%). We report output tokens per
second per GPU, the mean of three runs unless marked; the run-to-run
spread on the H100 is 1.4% (median) and 5.7% (95th percentile) with V2
and 2.5%/11.2% with V1, and at most 4.1% and 6.5% on the T4 and A10G. We
treat gaps below about 2% as ties. Unless stated otherwise the
controller uses hysteresis $`h=8`$ and rebuilds the table every 200
steps; the workload-switch runs use its defaults ($`h=4`$, every 500
steps) with exploration every 50 steps and prior decay 0.5. Draft
lengths and acceptance reported in the evaluation come from the same
vLLM metrics, read from each server’s /metrics endpoint, so every number
can be checked against vLLM’s own accounting.

#### Baselines.

_Best fixed_ at a load is the fastest fixed draft length there, without
a table and with full graphs, chosen after the fact; losses are against
it. _Best single fixed length_ is the one length with the smallest
worst-case loss over all loads, also chosen after the fact: an operator
would have to benchmark every length to find it. We credit TableTune
only with differences from such speculative configurations (and from
vLLM’s documented table and the adaptive baselines of
Section [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Q2: against prior adaptive control ‣ 6 Evaluation"));
what speculation gains over decoding without it is the drafter’s, not
the tuner’s, and we show it only for context.

| EAGLE-3, Spec-Bench chat     | 3.1^(§) | 3.9 (3)    | 39.3    | 2.5 (2)    | T4         | 3.8       | 2.2 (2)            |

(Section [6.7](#S6.SS7 "6.7 Q6: cost and reliability of measuring ‣ 6 Evaluation")).

Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.2 Q1: measured tables against fixed lengths ‣ 6 Evaluation")
is the main result. For each GPU it compares the tuned table’s worst
loss with that of the one fixed length an operator would have to find by
benchmarking every length.

_On the H100 with V2_, the tuned tables stay within 3.0–5.7% of the best
fixed length at every load for EAGLE-3, the 4-bit target, n-gram and
Spec-Bench, and within 11.6% for DFlash, whose best single fixed length
loses 19.1%. Here a well-chosen single length is nearly as safe: 3.4%
for EAGLE-3, and for n-gram and Spec-Bench the tuner itself returns one
length, the one an exhaustive benchmark picks (5 and 3). So on one H100
up to 128 requests the table’s value is that it finds that length
without benchmarking every length. Where no single length works, the
table keeps finding the right one: beyond 128 requests, where in llm-d
fixed length 3 falls up to 24% behind it
(Section [6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5 Q4: end to end in llm-d ‣ 6 Evaluation"));
on a mixture-of-experts target, with DFlash, and on the older GPUs
(below).

_A mixture-of-experts target_ behaves differently. With Qwen3-30B-A3B
(30B parameters, 3B active per token) and its EAGLE-3 drafter on one
H100 with V2, the step without speculation grows from 4.7 ms at a batch
of 1 to 19.7 ms at 128, because a larger batch activates more experts,
while three draft tokens add 61% at a batch of 1 but only 31% at 128,
once those experts are loaded. Speculation therefore keeps paying as
load grows: length 3 is the fastest fixed length at every load from 2 to
96 requests and length 2 at 128 (by 2.3%), and the tuner finds that
table ($`[[1,3,3],[4,4,2],[5,128,3]]`$), within 2.9% of the best fixed
length at every load. A table written for a dense model does not fit
here: vLLM’s documented table switches to length 1 above 64 requests and
loses 17.5% at 96 and 12.2% at 128 requests (three runs).

_Long prompts_ change the table less. With GovReport prompts [Huang
et al. (2021)](#bib.bib11) of 1,024 and 3,072 tokens (EAGLE-3, three
runs), the re-profiled table moves its edge from a batch of 50 to 36–38
and stays within 0.7% and 1.5% of the best fixed length, but the
32-token table (2.0%) and vLLM’s documented table (2.3%) do nearly as
well: on the H100 the step grows slowly enough that prompt length barely
matters.

_On the older GPUs_, for full-precision targets on the code workloads,
the tables stay within 2.3–5.2% where the best single fixed length loses
7.6–18.0%, and every fixed length loses 7.6–43.6% at some load.

_On the H100 with the default V1 runner_, the same kind of table loses
30–43% for every model-based drafter (n-gram, which adds no model pass,
5.2%): the cost of the engine’s graph mode, not of the tuner’s choices
(Section [6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Q5: what the engine must provide ‣ 6 Evaluation")).

#### Jumping load.

We drove one server per configuration through eleven 50-second windows
whose open requests jump between 2 and 128 (three runs). On the A10G the
tuned table never fell below 81% of the best configuration in a window
(mean 94.0%). On the H100 with V2 it was the best configuration in
practically every window: 98.5–100% of the per-window best (mean 99.6%),
4.1% above fixed length 1, 1.1% above the documented table and level
with fixed length 2 ($`-`$0.2%). With V1, fixed length 2 beat it by 15%.

#### Open-loop arrivals.

We also sent requests at 2 to 72 per second with Poisson and with bursty
arrivals (gamma inter-arrival times, smoothness 0.25), on the H100 with
V2, three runs each. Below saturation the draft length shows in latency,
and no single fixed length is right at every rate: at 2 requests per
second the median request takes 0.63–0.64 s with the tuned table and
fixed length 3 and 18% longer with length 1; at 72 per second the table
takes 1.08 s, length 1 1.10 s and length 3 22–24% longer. Bursty
arrivals change none of these orderings.

### 6.3 Q2: against prior adaptive control

Figure 3: TableTune against TurboSpec-style and Nightjar-style control
on the H100 (V2 runner), code prompts at temperature 1.0, mean of three
runs. Throughput as % of the best fixed draft length at each load; every
method chooses among the lengths of its starting table: with EAGLE-3,
0/1/3 for TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style, 2/3 for the all-length tuned
table and 1/3 for the 0/1/3 table (also the controller’s start); with
DFlash, 2/4/6/8 for all.

#### Baselines.

TurboSpec and Nightjar released no code, so we reimplemented each as a
vLLM plugin following its paper, in its own package that shares no code
with TableTune. _TurboSpec-style_ picks the length every step, for the
whole batch, maximizing goodput from a linear step-time model (a target
pass over $`B(k{+}1)`$ tokens plus $`k`$ drafting passes) fitted to the
tuner’s profile at eight batch sizes, and from one per-token acceptance
rate, a moving average over steps, with the geometric formula for tokens
per step [Liu et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib24). _Nightjar-style_ runs
Nightjar’s ADA-BINGREEDY bandit for every batch size, with the measured
time per output token as its loss [Li et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib16);
offloading the drafter to CPU memory needs engine changes and is
omitted. Both start from the tuner’s acceptance profile where they use
one, and, like TableTune’s controller, may only choose lengths that are
in their starting table, the only ones with full CUDA graphs under V2.

#### Results.

With EAGLE-3
(Figure [3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 6.3 Q2: against prior adaptive control ‣ 6 Evaluation")a)
the tuned tables stay within 3.3% (all-length table) and 3.7% (0/1/3
table) of the best fixed length at every load, 3.0% with the controller,
TurboSpec-style within 9.3% and Nightjar-style within 11.8%.
TurboSpec-style matches the tables up to 32 requests and then keeps
length 3 too long: its linear model ranks length 3 first up to a batch
of about 100, while the measured profile switches to length 2 above 50,
because the fit smooths over the jump in length-3 step time (at a batch
of 80, measured 9.7 ms, fitted 8.0 ms). The same choice makes its
requests 20–23% slower than with the table at 72 open-loop requests per
second. Nightjar-style loses 4–12% at every load because each batch size
learns separately and keeps exploring. With DFlash
(Figure [3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 6.3 Q2: against prior adaptive control ‣ 6 Evaluation")b)
all three trail fixed length 3 by 10–29% above 32 requests, a length
none of them has: the tuned table uses 2/4/6/8 and predicted length 4 to
beat 3 there, which the measured sweep contradicts
(Section [6.7](#S6.SS7 "6.7 Q6: cost and reliability of measuring ‣ 6 Evaluation")
explains why); among the three, TableTune loses least (15.8%, against
17.1% and 28.5%). In a repeat of the jumping-load study that adds the
two baselines (greedy, three runs), the tuned tables never fall below
95% of the best configuration in a window (the all-length table: 98%;
98.8–99.2% on average); TurboSpec-style and Nightjar-style fall to 89%
and 92% in the high-load windows and deliver 5.3% and 4.1% fewer tokens
in total than the all-length table. With greedy acceptance fixed length
2 is nearly as good as the tables here (98.3% on average).

#### vLLM’s adaptive verification.

vLLM’s *adaptive verification* [Wilkinson & Chislett
(2026)](#bib.bib39); [Delfin (2026)](#bib.bib6) picks at every step how
many drafted tokens of each request to verify, from a startup cost
profile and acceptance predicted from the draft logits; it needs the V2
runner and variable-length attention, and does not support n-gram
drafting, LoRA or pipeline parallelism. On vLLM main of October 20, 2026
(EAGLE-3, 1–128 requests, three runs), the tuner, rerun in 6 minutes,
gives $`[[1,36,3],[37,128,2]]`$, within 3.4% of the best fixed length at
every load (3.1% with the controller; fixed length 2: 4.1%). Adaptive
verification with up to 3 tokens trails the best fixed length by up to
26.2% and fixed length 3 by 7–26% at 2–64 requests, accepting 0.95
tokens per draft against 1.11. It was designed for confidence-head
drafters on large mixture-of-experts models, so this one-model result is
preliminary.

#### Repairing mistuned tables.

A table is _mistuned_ when its ranges or lengths do not fit the GPU,
drafter or workload it serves. The most natural case is vLLM’s
documented table, deployed as an operator copies it. In llm-d with
Qwen3-32B it drops to length 0 above a batch of 128 per replica, and
started from it the controller raises throughput by 9–29% at 256–1024
open requests, to the tuned table’s level
(Section [6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5 Q4: end to end in llm-d ‣ 6 Evaluation"));
on one H100 up to 128 requests the same table is nearly right, and the
controller adds only 2%. To test repair under larger errors,
Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 6.4 Q3: the controller ‣ 6 Evaluation") and
Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.4 Q3: the controller ‣ 6 Evaluation")
also start it from deliberately mistuned tables, with an acceptance
prior measured on a different workload. From the documented table with
its ranges divided by 4, which drops to length 0 above a batch of 32, it
gains up to 58% on the H100 (V2) and 45% (V1), against 36% on the T4 and
14% on the A10G: the H100’s wider gap between speculation and none makes
a mistuned table costlier and its repair larger. At every load and on
every GPU it reaches 96–103% of the tuned table’s throughput
(Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.4 Q3: the controller ‣ 6 Evaluation")a,
circles). On the mixture-of-experts target the same mistuned table costs
far more, because speculation pays at every load there: the controller
raises throughput by 71–83% at 40–96 requests (three runs), again to the
tuned table’s level. Started from another drafter’s table it rebuilds
the right one: +23% for DFlash on the H100 with V2, reaching the tuned
table’s throughput with only the starting table’s lengths 1–3 (V2 has
full graphs only for those), and +37% under V1, where it may use any
profiled length. At loads where the starting table is already
near-optimal it changes throughput by $`-`$3.7 to +3%. Under V1 on the
H100’s 4-bit target it costs 9–24% (single run, a launch-bound step);
under V2 the cost disappears.

#### A workload switch.

We switched the prompts mid-run between Spec-Bench math and translation,
the pair whose tables differ most, at the load where they disagree (80
open requests on the A10G and the H100 with V2, 71 with V1); after the
switch the first workload’s table is _stale_. On the A10G, where
translation’s table runs length 0 and math’s length 2 there, the stale
table loses 7.5–18.1%; the controller with its defaults oscillates or
stays at length 0, where it observes nothing, while with exploration and
prior decay it recovers 72% and 85% of the gap and rebuilds math’s table
exactly. We therefore recommend both options as defaults. On the H100
the same EAGLE-3 switch leaves little to recover ($`-`$4.5 to 1.5%,
Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 6.4 Q3: the controller ‣ 6 Evaluation")):
EAGLE-3’s acceptance varies too little across workloads for its H100
tables to differ much. DFlash’s varies far more (5.03 tokens per step at
length 8 on math, 2.51 on translation), so we repeated the switch with
DFlash, code then math at 96 open requests, where code’s table runs
length 2 and math’s length 6
(Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.4 Q3: the controller ‣ 6 Evaluation")b).
The stale code table loses 10.8% after the switch (three runs); the
controller rebuilds math’s table within the first minute and recovers
96% of the gap (+11.7%, within 0.4% of math’s own table), and before the
switch it beats code’s own table by 1.5% by learning that length 4 pays
at this load. TurboSpec-style also recovers it (+12.4%), since it too
tracks acceptance online; Nightjar-style recovers 38%, because its
bandit has to relearn every batch size. From translation to math at 48
requests the tables differ (length 4 against 8) but their throughput
does not ($`-`$1.1%), and every controller stays within 0.6% of math’s
own table.

### 6.5 Q4: end to end in llm-d

Figure 5: llm-d optimized-baseline with EAGLE-3 behind the llm-d router,
code prompts at temperature 1.0, mean of three runs: output tokens/s
against fixed draft length 3 (0 = fixed length 3). (a) The guide’s own
model and layout, 2 $`\times`$ Qwen3-32B at TP=2 on four H100s. (b) 4
$`\times`$ Qwen3-8B at TP=1 on the same GPUs; the 32-request dip is
shared by every speculative configuration. The tuned table with the
controller is within 2% of the table alone up to 512 requests in (b),
and up to 4% above it in (a); it is omitted.

#### Setup.

llm-d’s optimized-baseline guide [llm-d contributors (2026)](#bib.bib25)
serves vLLM replicas behind the llm-d router, an Envoy proxy with an
endpoint picker that routes by prefix-cache affinity and token load. We
deployed the guide as shipped, two replicas of Qwen3-32B at TP=2 on four
H100s with the guide’s Helm values for the router, which are calibrated
for this setup, and changed only configuration: a Kustomize overlay on
the guide’s model-server base adds the model’s EAGLE-3 drafter and the
tuned table to --speculative-config, uses a vLLM nightly image with the
V2 runner, caps each replica at 256 sequences of 4096 tokens, and for
the controller puts the TableTune package on PYTHONPATH and sets its
VLLM_DSD\_\* variables; the overlay is in the repository. The tuner
profiled one replica at TP=2 with the same image in about 30 minutes;
its all-length table steps from length 2 to 1, which stalls this nightly
(Section [6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Q5: what the engine must provide ‣ 6 Evaluation")),
so we deploy its 0/1/3 table, $`[[1,60,3],[61,256,1]]`$. As a second
scale we ran four Qwen3-8B replicas at TP=1 on the same GPUs. AIPerf
sent code prompts through the router at 4–1024 open requests, three runs
per configuration (run-to-run spread 3.2% median).

#### Results.

On the guide as shipped
(Figure [5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.5 Q4: end to end in llm-d ‣ 6 Evaluation")a),
up to 128 open requests the tuned table runs length 3 and matches fixed
length 3 and the documented table within run-to-run noise. From 256 the
replicas cross the table’s edge to length 1, and there it is 20–32%
faster than fixed length 3 and 7–25% faster than the documented table,
which drops to length 0 above a batch of 128 per replica; at 512 and
1024 open requests the median time between tokens is 23–29% lower than
with either, and the median first token arrives 23–26% sooner at 1024.
(Speculation itself, with any of these configurations, adds 48–78% over
the guide as shipped at up to 64 requests; that gain belongs to the
drafter.) Started from the documented table, the controller raised
throughput by 9–29% at 256–1024 open requests, to the tuned table’s
level, and on top of the tuned table it added up to 4%. With four
Qwen3-8B replicas
(Figure [5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.5 Q4: end to end in llm-d ‣ 6 Evaluation")b)
the table is up to 22% faster than fixed length 3 (5% behind it at 1024)
and up to 40% faster than the documented table, and the controller adds
14% and 39% to the latter at 512 and 1024 requests.

### 6.6 Q5: what the engine must provide

#### Full CUDA graphs per draft length.

On vLLM’s default V1 runner any table switches the decode step to
piecewise CUDA graphs, which add CPU launch work to every step (a Nsight
trace on the T4 shows the GPU busy 91% of the time with full graphs and
60% with piecewise ones). A long step hides that work, as on the older
GPUs; the H100’s step is short (about 6 ms for Qwen3-4B), so it shows:
piecewise graphs alone cost fixed length 3 24–34% at 1–32 requests, more
host cores do not help (2, 4 or 16), and host contention makes it worse.
With V2’s full graphs per draft length the loss disappears
(Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.2 Q1: measured tables against fixed lengths ‣ 6 Evaluation")).
Until an engine provides them, keep a table only if it beats the best
fixed length and no speculation, both timed with full graphs.

#### Length switches that do not stall.

On this vLLM nightly, several tables that step from length 2 to length 1
stalled the V2 runner under load (the 4-bit target’s tuned table,
EAGLE-3’s T4 table, translation’s table, and llm-d’s at its 80/81 edge).
The 0/1/3 tables, and tables without such a step, never stalled; we
report those where marked, and the fault upstream.

#### A real off switch.

A table entry of 0 still runs EAGLE-style drafters, which keep their own
KV cache: where no speculation is best (the A10G above 96 requests) the
tuned table trails it by 5.6–6.7%, and on the H100 a table at length 0
runs 19–22% below no speculation. Nightjar [Li et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib16) provides one.

### 6.7 Q6: cost and reliability of measuring

#### Overheads.

Profiling takes 8 minutes on the H100 (20 for the mixture-of-experts
target, 28 for Qwen3-32B at TP=2, 22 on the A10G, 45 on the T4), once
per GPU, engine, model and drafter; a new workload needs only a 2-minute
acceptance profile. The controller adds no GPU work.

#### Measure, do not fit.

Step times must be measured per GPU and engine. On the H100 a linear
model misses a jump in length-3 step time and costs TurboSpec-style
control 9%
(Section [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Q2: against prior adaptive control ‣ 6 Evaluation"));
on the A10G every simple model we fitted misses the switch to length 0
and loses 12.7% at 128 requests.

#### Where the profile misses: DFlash.

Timing with every guess rejected does not time work that grows with
accepted tokens. For DFlash that matters: its acceptance in the sweep
matches the profile, but at length 8 its steps take 1.3–1.9$`\times`$
the profiled time at live batches of 6–38, against 1.05–1.16$`\times`$
at length 1. Profiling with the measured acceptance instead (vLLM’s
synthetic rejection sampler, steps counted from its draft counter)
corrects the step times but barely changes the table: in both profiles
length 3 wins only in short ranges above a batch of about 47, which the
25% minimum-width rule merges into length 4. A tolerance repairs this:
merge a narrow range only if that loses less than 2% of its predicted
goodput, our tie threshold. It changes four of our V2 tables; rerun
against the original ones in the same session (three runs), it makes
DFlash 6.5% faster at 64 requests, n-gram about 5% faster at 96–128 and
Spec-Bench 3% faster at 64, and leaves EAGLE-3 within noise; the other
tables do not change. It is a tuner option (--merge-tol); the results
above use the original rule. DFlash still trails fixed length 3 by 10%
at 128 requests, serving work such as interleaved prefill that a
decode-only profile cannot see.

#### Near-ties and an invalid profile.

With EAGLE-3 on the H100, lengths 2 and 3 nearly tie, and two profiles
of the same GPU differed by 4–9% in single step times, enough to move an
edge at a cost of a few percent. Under V2 the profile of the Qwen3-0.6B
draft model is flat at about 40 ms, against 9–37 ms when served, so that
table is invalid.

## 7 Limitations

#### Engines.

The results with full graphs use one vLLM nightly, whose V2 runner
stalls when a table steps from length 2 to 1
(Section [6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 Q5: what the engine must provide ‣ 6 Evaluation"));
where that matters, including both llm-d deployments, we report the
0/1/3 table, which can be slightly worse than the all-length table.

#### Accuracy of the table.

The tuner’s choices are only as good as its profiles. With DFlash the
table loses up to 16% to fixed length 3 at batches of 34–87; a merge
tolerance repairs part of it, but serving work the profile cannot see
leaves a 10% gap at 128 requests
(Section [6.7](#S6.SS7 "6.7 Q6: cost and reliability of measuring ‣ 6 Evaluation")),
and the controller, whose prior was accurate, does not correct cost
errors. The draft model’s V2 profile was invalid, and its T4 results at
high load are decided by KV-cache pressure and preemption, which the
step-time profile cannot see.

#### Scope.

Dense targets of 4B, 8B and 32B parameters and one mixture-of-experts
target with 3B active parameters, on H100s in a single node at TP of at
most 2; prompts of 32 tokens in most studies and of up to 3,072 tokens
in one, answers up to 256 tokens (512 for n-gram); closed-loop load,
plus open-loop arrivals up to 72 requests per second on one GPU. Prompts
beyond 4,096 tokens, mixed and recorded traffic, larger
mixture-of-experts models, multi-node and disaggregated serving are
missing. TurboSpec and Nightjar released no code; our reimplementations
omit Nightjar’s drafter offloading and TurboSpec’s context-length term.
We compare runs only within a node and session.

## 8 Related Work

#### Drafters and per-request adaptation.

Drafter designs [Li et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib17); [Li et al.
(2024c)](#bib.bib18); [Li et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib19); [Cai et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib2); [Miao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib27); [Chen et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib5); [Saxena (2023)](#bib.bib35); [Fu et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib7); [Chen et al. (2026)](#bib.bib4) and methods that
adapt the length per request or token [Mamou et al. (2024)](#bib.bib26);
[Huang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib9); [Agrawal et al. (2024)](#bib.bib1);
[Hou et al. (2025)](#bib.bib8); [Liu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib22); [Zhang
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib45) or update the drafter online [Liu et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib23) are complementary to choosing the length from load.

#### Load-aware speculation in serving.

Su et al. [Su et al. (2023)](#bib.bib37) proposed choosing the
speculation length per batch size, the idea behind vLLM’s Dynamic SD
table. BASS [Qian et al. (2024)](#bib.bib31) batches speculation,
TETRIS [Wu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib41) picks which draft tokens to verify
across a batch, and Sequoia [Chen et al. (2024)](#bib.bib5) sizes its
token tree for the hardware. TurboSpec [Liu et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib24)
is closest to our work: it maximizes goodput inside vLLM with a linear
step-time model fitted to profiled runs and a moving average of recent
acceptance, choosing the length at each step. TableTune applies these
ideas to vLLM’s production table, measures the grid instead of fitting
it, and keeps the table current with a plugin;
Section [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Q2: against prior adaptive control ‣ 6 Evaluation")
compares it with reimplementations of TurboSpec and Nightjar.
Nightjar [Li et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib16) picks the length per batch size
online with a multi-armed bandit, switches speculation truly off and
moves the drafter to CPU memory. vLLM’s adaptive verification [Wilkinson
& Chislett (2026)](#bib.bib39); [Delfin (2026)](#bib.bib6) sizes the
verified drafts per request and step from a profiled cost model and
predicted acceptance
(Section [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Q2: against prior adaptive control ‣ 6 Evaluation")).
SpecServe/AdaSpec [Huang et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib10) and AdaServe [Li
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib20) adapt speculation to latency targets; we
optimize throughput. MagicDec [Sadhukhan et al. (2025)](#bib.bib34)
finds speculation pays at large batches for long contexts, and Kong et
al. [Kong et al. (2026)](#bib.bib12) model its latency under load.

## 9 Conclusion

A draft-length table must be measured for each GPU, engine and model and
kept current as traffic changes; TableTune measures it in minutes and
repairs it while serving. On an H100 with full CUDA graphs its tables
stay within 3–6% of the best fixed length for most drafters, with lower
worst-case loss than reimplemented TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control
and vLLM’s adaptive verification. Its controller recovers up to 58% from
mistuned tables, and in llm-d’s optimized-baseline guide as shipped the
tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length and 25% faster
than vLLM’s documented table.

Tables do not transfer (a dense-model table loses up to 18% on a
mixture-of-experts model); engines need full graphs per draft length,
stall-free switches and a real off switch.

During the preparation of this work, Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet was used
to assist the authors in summarizing preliminary literature during the
background phase and structuring the initial outline of the related work
section. The tool was also used to generate boilerplate Python scripts
for rendering the graphs. Anthropic’s Claude Code was used for
submission formatting checks. The authors manually scrutinized all
generated scripts, conducted the actual evaluations, and independently
drafted the final text. The authors take full responsibility for the
